shots: busy open-air market in Abidjan Ivory Coast at early morning, colorful wax print fabrics, stalls with fish and attieke, yellow taxis, golden light, crowd blurred, no readable signs
mom
My name is Grace Kouassi. I sell fish and attiéké at the Adjamé market in Abidjan. And last year I learned that God stays faithful even when people don't.

a 40 year old Ivorian woman with dark brown skin, wearing a colorful wax print dress and matching headwrap, smiling while serving attieke and grilled fish at her market stall, wooden table, plastic bowls, warm morning light, Abidjan market
mom
For twelve years I've gotten up at four in the morning. My husband Koffi drives a shared taxi. Between the two of us, we keep the house going.
mom
My daughter Bénédicte is fourteen. She wants to be a doctor. My little Josué is nine. He just wants to play football.

a group of twelve Ivorian market women in colorful wax print dresses sitting in a circle on plastic chairs under a tree, one woman holding a notebook, cash envelopes, laughing together, warm afternoon light
mom
Like a lot of women at the market, I was in a savings circle. Twelve women. Every week, each one puts in ten thousand francs. And every month, one of us gets the whole pot.
mom
My turn was in September. Just in time for school. Bénédicte's school fees, supplies, uniforms. I had it all worked out.
a 50 year old Ivorian woman in an elegant wax print dress and gold earrings holding a thick notebook and cash envelope, confident smile, standing at a market stall, warm light
mom
Auntie Odile kept the money. We sang together in the church choir. She held my Josué the day he was baptized. I trusted her like a big sister.
a 40 year old Ivorian woman in a wax print dress standing in front of a closed metal shop shutter with a padlock, holding her phone to her ear, shocked worried face, market street, midday
mom
On the day of my turn, Auntie Odile didn't come. Her phone was off. Her shop was closed.
mom
The next day we found out she was gone. With everything. More than a million francs. Twelve families' money.
a 40 year old Ivorian woman sitting alone on a wooden bench in a small modest living room at night, head in her hands, a school uniform folded beside her, single light bulb, emotional
mom
That night I didn't tell the children anything. I sat in the living room with Bénédicte's uniform next to me. And I felt the anger rising.
mom
Not just about the money. About the shame. I had trusted her. The whole market was going to talk.
two Ivorian market women talking quietly at a stall, one leaning in and whispering with a serious expression, the other listening uncomfortably, colorful fabrics behind, afternoon
mom
A neighbor from the market came to see me. She whispered, Grace, I know someone. A marabout. He can make her come back, or make her pay.
mom
I won't lie. For one second, I wanted to say yes.
an open French Bible on a wooden table next to a small kerosene lamp at night, soft warm light on the pages, no people, shallow depth of field
verse
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord. Romans twelve, nineteen.
a 40 year old Ivorian woman in a headwrap sitting at night on a bench holding a smartphone, typing, tears on her cheeks, the screen glow on her face, modest home
mom
That night I opened the app my cousin in Paris had sent me. Community Covenant. There's a box that asks, how are you?
mom
I wrote, someone stole my children's school money. It was a sister from church. I want revenge. I don't recognize myself.
close up of a smartphone screen in a woman's hands showing a warm chat reply, soft glow, blurred living room background, no readable text
reply
Grace, your anger is real, and God hears it. You don't have to pretend it doesn't hurt.
reply
But don't let this betrayal steal your peace too. Hand justice over to God, and ask him for the next step, not the whole road.
a 14 year old Ivorian girl with dark skin and neat braids, wearing a school uniform, standing in a doorway of a modest home at night, looking at her mother with concern
mom
Bénédicte had heard me crying. She sat down next to me and said, Mama, I can wait a year. It's okay.
mom
That broke my heart. A fourteen-year-old who wants to carry her mother's weight.
an Ivorian mother hugging her teenage daughter on a bench in a modest living room at night, the mother's eyes closed, single warm light bulb, emotional
mom
I took her in my arms and said, no, my daughter. That's not yours to carry. I will do my part, and God will do his.
a 55 year old Ivorian pastor with short grey hair wearing a simple shirt and glasses sitting with a woman in wax print on plastic chairs in a small church courtyard, listening kindly, morning light
mom
On Sunday I went to see Pastor Yao. I thought he would tell me to forgive right away and forget everything.
pastor
Grace, forgiving doesn't mean saying it was nothing. It means refusing to make revenge your job. Judgment belongs to God. Your job is your children.
a group of Ivorian market women in wax print dresses standing together in a church courtyard holding hands in a circle praying, eyes closed, morning sunlight
mom
And then he did something I didn't expect. He gathered the eleven women from the savings circle after service. We prayed together. Not against Odile. For our children.
mom
One of us said, if we stay alone, we stay robbed. If we stand together, we start again.
a 40 year old Ivorian woman in a wax print dress sitting across a desk from a school principal in a modest school office in Abidjan, papers on the desk, respectful conversation, daylight
mom
On Monday I went to see the school principal. I was ashamed, but I told the truth. She let me pay in three installments.
a 40 year old Ivorian woman frying fish and serving customers at a busy market stall at evening under string lights, her teenage daughter in a school uniform helping count coins, warm light
mom
I added evenings at the market. Bénédicte came to help me after school, with her notebooks on the table between customers.
verse
Commit thy way unto the Lord; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass. Psalm thirty-seven, five.
an older Ivorian woman in a plain dress with a headwrap standing ashamed at a market stall at dusk, holding out an envelope with both hands, eyes down, another woman facing her silently
mom
Seven months later, Auntie Odile came back. Thin. She said her son got sick in Bouaké, that she panicked, that she lost everything.
mom
She handed me an envelope. It wasn't all of it. But it was a start.
two Ivorian women in their forties and fifties standing face to face at dusk in a market, one placing a hand gently on the other's shoulder, solemn, tears, warm light
mom
I haven't forgotten. I will never trust her with a pot again. But I told her, I forgive you. And I felt a weight fall off my shoulders.
a 14 year old Ivorian girl in a crisp school uniform with braids walking through a school gate in the morning, backpack on, smiling, other students around, Abidjan
mom
Bénédicte didn't lose her school year. She's in ninth grade now, top of her class in science. She still says she'll be a doctor. I believe her.
a 40 year old Ivorian woman in a wax print dress and headwrap standing at her market stall at sunrise, looking at the camera with a calm strong smile, colorful market behind
mom
I'm telling you this because betrayal happens to everyone. A sister, a friend, a husband, a boss. And the devil always comes with two offers. Revenge, or giving up.
mom
